cues.text: A differential equation relates an unknown function to one or more of its
derivatives.
In an ordinary differential equation the function depends on one independent
variable, such as y depending on x.
A prime usually means differentiation with respect to that independent
variable: y prime means d y over d x, and y double prime means the second
derivative.
The order is the highest derivative order actually present in the equation.
In y double prime plus three y prime plus two y equal to zero, the order is
two.
In the cube of y prime equal to x plus y, the order is one.
Cubing a first derivative does not make it a third derivative.
Before classifying a written equation, simplify exact cancellations so that a
term that disappears is not counted.
An equation containing partial derivatives belongs to a different category and
is outside this class.
The original equation also carries domain restrictions.
For example, a denominator x excludes zero even if an expression is later
simplified on an allowed interval.
State which variable is independent and which function is unknown before
reading either the notation or the solution.
Degree concerns algebraic powers of derivatives, rather than the highest
derivative order.
It is defined when the equation can be expressed as a polynomial in the
derivatives after valid removal of fractions and radicals involving
derivatives.
The degree is the power of the highest order derivative in that polynomial
form.
In the square of y double prime plus the cube of y prime plus y equal to zero,
the order is two and the degree is two.
The cube on the lower derivative does not determine the degree.
The cube of y prime equal to x plus y instead has order one and degree three.
In y double prime plus sine of y prime equal to zero, the derivative appears
inside a trigonometric function, so its degree is not defined.
A sine of x or a sine of y alone does not create that same obstacle because
neither is a sine of a derivative.
When squaring a derivative radical or clearing a derivative denominator,
record
any sign or nonzero conditions required for equivalence.
Otherwise the transformed equation may acquire solutions that do not satisfy
the original equation.
Always check a proposed solution in the original relation.
Solving a differential equation means finding functions that satisfy it on an
interval.
For y prime equal to two x, direct integration gives y equal to x squared plus
C.
The constant is arbitrary, so this is a family of solutions.
A particular initial condition selects a member when it is compatible with the
equation.
If y of one is three, substituting gives three equal to one plus C, so C is
two.
The selected solution is y equal to x squared plus two.
Verify it in two separate ways: its derivative must equal the right hand side
for every input in the chosen interval, and its value at the initial input
must
equal the stated value.
A function that merely passes through the initial point need not solve the
equation.
A formula that satisfies the equation away from a pole cannot be declared a
solution on an interval containing that pole.
First order equations often yield one integration constant, but that
observation is not a replacement for verification or a universal existence
claim.
Nonlinear equations can also have exceptional solutions that a division step
misses.
Keep such candidates until the original equation has been tested.
Eliminating arbitrary constants provides one way to form a differential
equation from a family of curves.
Consider y equal to C times e to the two x.
Differentiation gives y prime equal to two C times e to the two x.
Replace the repeated expression C times e to the two x by y, obtaining y prime
minus two y equal to zero.
No division by y is needed, so the member with C equal to zero remains
included.
For the family of straight lines y equal to A x plus B, one differentiation
gives y prime equal to A.
A second differentiation eliminates A as well, giving y double prime equal to
zero.
Conversely, integrating that last equation twice recovers the full line family
on an interval.
The number of independent constants suggests how many differentiations may be
useful in a nondegenerate family.
It does not justify blindly differentiating every formula a fixed number of
times without elimination.
If the family contains parameters that are not independent, or if a
manipulation divides by an expression that can vanish, inspect those cases
separately.
Formation is a supporting technique here; the main solution methods are
separation, homogeneous substitution and linear integrating factors.
A separable equation can be written as y prime equal to a function of x times
a
function of y.
On an interval where the y factor is nonzero, move that factor to the y side
and integrate each side in its own variable.
For y prime equal to x y, division by y gives d y over y equal to x d
x.
Integration gives natural log of absolute y equal to x squared over two plus a
constant.
Exponentiating and absorbing the nonzero magnitude and sign into a new
constant
gives y equal to C times e to the x squared over two for nonzero C.
The division excluded y equal to zero, so test that function in the original
equation.
It also satisfies y prime equal to x y.
Including C equal to zero now represents it in the final family.
A logarithmic intermediate constant and the final multiplicative constant are
not the same parameter, even when both are conventionally named C.
For an initial value y of zero equal to two, the multiplicative constant is
two.
Differentiate the resulting exponential to check that the inner derivative x
restores the original right hand side.
For y prime equal to y squared, the equation is separable.
When y is nonzero, integrate y to the negative two with respect to y to obtain
negative one over y equal to x plus a constant.
The initial condition y of zero equal to one gives the constant negative one.
Solving for y produces one divided by one minus x.
Its derivative is one divided by the square of one minus x, which equals y
squared wherever the denominator is nonzero.
The formula has a pole at x equal to one.
The maximal interval containing the initial input zero is therefore all x less
than one.
The same algebraic formula on x greater than one does not extend the initial
solution across the pole.
Division by y also excluded the constant solution y equal to zero; verify and
restore it when describing the original equation's solutions.
An equation that looks simple can thus produce a finite input where a solution
becomes unbounded.
The answer should include both the explicit function and the interval
associated with the initial condition, rather than just the rational
expression
alone.
Separation can produce inverse trigonometric integrals as well as logarithms.
For y prime equal to two x times the quantity one plus y squared, divide by
one
plus y squared.
This factor is strictly positive for real y, so this division loses no real
constant solution.
Integrating gives arctangent y equal to x squared plus an integration constant
on a suitable branch interval.
The initial condition y of zero equal to zero selects constant zero near the
initial point.
Taking tangent gives y equal to tangent of x squared.
The interval containing zero must stop before x squared reaches pi over two,
because tangent has a pole there.
Thus absolute x must be less than square root of pi over two.
Differentiate on this interval: y prime is two x times secant squared of x
squared, which equals two x times one plus y squared.
Although tangent is periodic, an initial solution cannot be continued through
one of its infinite poles by switching branches.
State the local inverse convention used in the integration and verify the
explicit solution on the interval selected by its initial data.
A first order homogeneous ratio equation has right hand side depending only on
y over x, on a region where x is nonzero.
This use of homogeneous is different from the word homogeneous in a linear
equation with zero forcing term.
For y prime equal to one plus y over x, set v equal to y over x, or y equal to
v x.
Here v depends on x.
The product rule gives y prime equal to v plus x times v prime.
Substituting produces v plus x v prime equal to one plus v.
The v terms cancel, leaving v prime equal to one over x.
Integration gives v equal to natural log of absolute x plus C, so y equals x
times the quantity natural log of absolute x plus C.
Differentiating this expression gives natural log of absolute x plus C plus
one, exactly one plus y over x.
Use an interval entirely on one side of zero, because the original equation
excludes x equal to zero.
Replacing y prime by only v would omit the derivative of the changing ratio
and
destroy the method.
Homogeneous substitution can introduce a division that hides straight line
solutions.
Consider y prime equal to the square of y over x, with x nonzero.
Put y equal to v x.
The transformed equation is x v prime equal to v squared minus v, or v times v
minus one.
Before dividing by that product, inspect its zeros.
Constant v equal to zero gives y equal to zero, and constant v equal to one
gives y equal to x.
Both solve the original equation on intervals excluding zero.
For the other branches, separation gives d v divided by v times v minus one
equal to d x over x.
Partial fractions integrate the left side to natural log of the absolute value
of the ratio v minus one to v.
Solving the resulting relation gives y equal to x divided by one minus C x.
Setting C equal to zero recovers y equal to x in this displayed family, while
y
equal to zero remains an additional solution.
Require both x nonzero and one minus C x nonzero.
Verification distinguishes an actually missing branch from one already
represented by a special value of the final constant.
A first order linear equation in y has the normalized form y prime plus P of x
times y equal to Q of x.
Neither P nor Q depends on y.
Choose an integrating factor mu equal to the exponential of an antiderivative
of P.
Its derivative equals P times mu.
Multiplying the equation by mu makes the left hand side the derivative of the
product mu y.
Integration then gives mu y equal to the integral of mu Q with respect to x,
plus C.
A nonzero constant multiplier in mu does not change the final solution family,
so one convenient integrating factor is enough.
For y prime plus two y equal to four, use mu equal to e to the two x.
Integration gives y equal to two plus C e to the negative two x.
If y of zero is three, C is one.
Differentiate and substitute to verify the decaying term cancels in y prime
plus two y.
The method requires normalization first.
If the coefficient of y prime vanishes somewhere, dividing by it restricts the
interval and that excluded location must be considered separately in the
original equation.
A variable coefficient equation should be normalized before its integrating
factor is read.
For x y prime plus y equal to two x, divide by x only on an interval where
x is nonzero.
The normalized equation is y prime plus y over x equal to two.
Integrating P equal to one over x gives natural log of absolute x, so the
positive exponential choice for mu is absolute x.
On either side of zero, x itself is also a valid nonzero constant multiple of
that factor, and is convenient.
Multiplication makes the equation the derivative of x y equal to two x.
Integrating gives x y equal to x squared plus C, hence y equal to x plus C
over
x.
If y of one equals three, C equals two and the initial solution lies on x
greater than zero.
Do not claim that every member passes through zero.
The member with C equal to zero can be extended as y equal to x and satisfies
the original unnormalized equation even there, but members with nonzero C have
a pole.
The original equation, rather than the divided form alone, decides what an
extension can mean.
Sometimes an equation is linear when x is treated as the dependent variable
and
y as the independent variable.
For d x over d y plus x equal to y, the unknown is a function x of y.
The coefficient of x is one, so the integrating factor is e to the y.
Multiplication gives the derivative with respect to y of the product e to the
y
times x equal to y e to the y.
Integration by parts gives the integral on the right as e to the y times the
quantity y minus one, plus C.
Dividing by e to the y gives x equal to y minus one plus C e to the negative
y.
The condition x of zero equal to one sets C equal to two.
Differentiate with respect to y to check that d x over d y plus x equals y.
Do not silently substitute d y over d x for d x over d y.
Reciprocating a derivative needs a local inverse and a nonzero derivative, and
may exclude points.
Keeping the chosen independent variable explicit is safer than assuming every
first order equation must be linear in y as a function of x.
A rate proportional to the current amount gives a simple separable
differential
equation.
For decay, write d N over d t equal to negative k N, with k
positive.
Separation or the linear method yields N equal to the initial amount times e
to
the negative k t.
The initial value is N of zero, and the model keeps a positive initial amount
positive at every finite time.
The coefficient k has inverse time units, so its product with t in the
exponent
is dimensionless.
A half life T means the amount at time T is one half of the initial amount.
Substitution gives e to the negative k T equal to one half, hence k equal to
natural log two divided by T.
After two half lives the remaining amount is one quarter, not zero.
For an initial amount eighty and half life three time units, the amount at
time
six is twenty.
Growth uses the positive sign instead and gives an increasing exponential for
a
positive initial amount.
The proportional rate assumption is a modelling choice; it should not be
inferred merely from one observed pair of amounts without stating that
assumption.
A reliable solution begins by classifying the equation after checking its
domain.
If the right hand side factors into a function of x times a function of y, try
separation and inspect the zeros of the factor divided out.
If the right hand side depends on y over x, use y equal to v x and the product
rule, then inspect any constant v branches excluded during separation.
If the normalized equation is linear in its chosen unknown, find the
integrating factor from the coefficient of that unknown.
These categories can overlap: y prime equal to x y is both separable and
linear.
Choosing either valid method should produce equivalent families on the same
interval.
They do not cover every differential equation.
For example, a nonlinear equation need not become separable just because it is
first order.
After integration, absorb constants only through valid operations, restore
exceptional solutions, and differentiate the candidate in the original
equation.
Then check the initial condition and identify the connected interval
containing
its input.
A pole, a logarithmic restriction or an excluded original denominator can end
that interval.
These checks are part of the solution, not optional finishing details after
the algebra.
